insights.tldr: Playoff rotations are way more stylistically diverse than lottery teams' — winners collect different weapons, not copies — but the spread doesn't predict how deep a run goes.
insights.title: Making the playoffs takes variety — surviving them takes matchups
insights.lede: Mean pairwise style distance among rotation players (≥1,000 min), 14-d embedding space, 1996-97 → 2024-25. Every tier of the playoffs draws from the same diverse pool — once you're in, style spread doesn't predict how far you go. Most-diverse champs: the 2014-15 Warriors (5.78), 2019-20 Lakers (5.62), 2010-11 Mavericks (5.62); tightest: the 1999-00 Lakers (4.10).
insights.stat_label: wider rotation style spread — playoff teams vs non-playoff (5.06 vs 4.82)
insights.viz_label: Mean rotation style spread by furthest round reached
insights.foot: 862 team-seasons; furthest round from playoff series records; 2025-26 excluded (season in progress).
insights.og_title: Winners don't look alike
insights.og_desc: Playoff rotations span 5% more style space — but Finals teams are no more diverse than first-round exits. Matchups decide.

insights.tldr: Playoff game plans erase pure shooters — scoring, usage and efficiency all crater — while playmakers are the only ones whose role grows. You can scheme a jumper in two days; not a creator.
insights.title: May solves shooters. It can't solve playmakers.
insights.lede: Playoff minus regular-season pts/100 by style archetype — 4,739 rotation player-seasons, 1996-97 → 2024-25. Pure 3-point specialists lose 2.3 pts/100 in May, with usage (-1.00) and true shooting (-0.039) falling too — worst of all eight archetypes. Playmakers are the only group whose role grows (usage +0.19), and 1 in 16 playoff teams is led in usage by a playmaker, up from 1 in 250 in the regular season. The pattern fits a game-planning story — a best-of-7 gives defenses time to scheme a jumper, not a creator — but that's the best-fit mechanism, not proven causation. Loudest single-postseason swings are small-sample color, but the 2026 Finals lived the pattern. The Knicks' title run rode its playmakers: Finals MVP Jalen Brunson averaged 32.6 points (45 in the closeout), and Jose Alvarado — just 4.2 points a night but a +18.9 on/off — sparked the 29-point Game 4 comeback with 8 fourth-quarter points. Spurs rookie creator Dylan Harper's role grew all series, up to 18.0 points per game off the bench from 11.8 in the regular season. At the other end, veteran shooter Harrison Barnes was squeezed out of the rotation in the Finals after 9.9 per game in the regular season. Even Victor Wembanyama's brilliant 26-a-night couldn't scheme-proof San Antonio alone.
insights.stat_label: playoff pts/100 drop for pure 3-point specialists (usage and efficiency fall too)
insights.viz_label: Playoff scoring change (pts/100) by style archetype
insights.foot: 4,739 rotation player-seasons (playoff GP ≥ 4, regular season ≥ 25 scaled min/g); regular-season vs playoff splits via stats.nba.com; 2025-26 excluded (season in progress).
insights.og_title: The playoffs eat shooters
insights.og_desc: Pure 3-point specialists lose 2.3 pts/100 in May — playmakers are the only ones whose role grows.

insights.tldr: Among established scorers, Donovan Mitchell owns the two biggest playoff scoring leaps of the last 30 years — and Joel Embiid owns the single biggest collapse (-14.6). May doesn't just test talent; it tests whose game translates.
insights.title: May makes some stars bigger — and shrinks others
insights.lede: Scoring-rate change from regular season to playoffs (pts/100) for established scorers: 28+ pts/100 across 40+ regular-season games, 8+ playoff games, and a real playoff role. 334 player-seasons qualified, 1996-97 → 2025-26. The risers: Mitchell's 2025 encore (+8.6) and his 2021 surge (+8.3), Duncan's 2006 throwback (+8.2), and a +7.2 tie for fourth between LeBron's 2009 rampage and Durant's pre-injury 2019 tear. The fallers: Embiid's 2023 collapse (-14.6, the largest in the sample) and his 2022 fade (-12.6), Porzingis's hollowed-out 2025 (-13.6), Jermaine O'Neal's 2005 fade (-13.2), and Jordan Clarkson's 2018 dip (-12.0).
insights.stat_label: Mitchell's 2025 scoring jump (pts/100) — the biggest rise among established scorers
insights.viz_label: Scoring change, regular season → playoffs (pts/100)
insights.foot: 334 established-scorer seasons (28+ RS pts/100, 40+ RS games, 8+ playoff games, playoff usage ≥ 18); regular-season vs playoff splits via stats.nba.com. This is the biggest swing in scoring rate — not the greatest postseason run; see the playoff-runs rankings for that.
insights.og_title: Playoff risers & fallers
insights.og_desc: Mitchell owns the two biggest May scoring leaps in 30 years. Embiid owns the biggest collapse.

insights.tldr: Five teams clear both bars — a playoff-shaped rotation and a top-10 engine: the Lakers, Oklahoma City, Denver, Philadelphia and Miami. Portland has the most playoff-shaped rotation in the league and no engine to match; the champs and runners-up win on talent, not shape.
insights.title: Who looks like a contender — and who looks lottery-shaped
insights.lede: Each projected 2026-27 rotation measured with the contender-chemistry metric (mean pairwise style distance in the 14-d embedding space), centered on the historical playoff-team mean of 5.06 — right of the line is playoff-shaped, left is lottery-shaped. Five teams clear both bars, shape and engine: the Lakers pair the second-most playoff-shaped rotation (5.56) with Dončić (38.1 pts/100); Oklahoma City (5.31, Gilgeous-Alexander 44.1); Denver (5.20, Jokić 37.1); Philadelphia (5.14, Brown 41.0 — plus LeBron, plus Embiid); and Miami (5.12, Antetokounmpo 42.7). The twist: last June's finalists both sit BELOW the line — the champion Knicks (4.80) and the Spurs (4.84) win on talent, not shape, exactly what the chemistry card predicted: variety gets you in, matchups decide the rest. The cautionary tale is Portland: the most playoff-shaped rotation in the league (5.67) with no top-10 engine — Sacramento (5.45), Utah (5.44) and Detroit (5.41) fit the same profile. At the bottom, Atlanta (4.06) has the most homogeneous rotation in the league. One asterisk from the risers & fallers card: Philadelphia's ceiling runs through Embiid, owner of the largest playoff scoring collapse of the last 30 years — and he has played 39% of possible games across the last three seasons.
insights.stat_label: Portland's spread above the playoff-team line — most playoff-shaped rotation, without a top-10 engine
insights.viz_label: 2026-27 rotation spread vs the playoff-team mean (5.06)

insights.tldr: 33 times since 1997, a high-usage star changed teams, took a much smaller piece of the offense — and won much bigger. Iguodala gave up 10.8 points of playoff usage and won Finals MVP as a sixth man; Gordon went from Orlando's playoff go-to guy to Denver's fourth option and a championship, more efficient on less.
insights.title: The fastest way to win more is to need the ball less
insights.lede: Usage sacrificed (regular-season or playoff USG, whichever shows the role change) against playoff rounds gained, for players who went from a team's hub (21.5+ USG) to its third option or lower on a different, much better team. Dwight Howard's −14.0 is the biggest sacrifice on a title team: Houston's hub to the Lakers' rim-runner at .677 true shooting. Rows are ranked by sacrifice × rounds gained, so JR Smith's record −14.6 sits sixth — his leap was three rounds, not four, and it came in a five-game 2011 cameo.
insights.stat_label: Dwight Howard's playoff-usage drop, Houston hub to Lakers rim-runner — the biggest sacrifice on a title team
insights.viz_label: Usage given up (USG points) × playoff rounds gained
insights.foot: 33 qualifying transitions, 1996-97 → 2025-26. Old season: 50+ RS games, 21.5+ USG (RS or playoffs), team won ≤ 1 round. New season: different team, 3rd option or lower, 8+ playoff games at 14+ USG and .520+ TS, efficiency held vs the old role, team won ≥ 2 more rounds. Pre-move stardom on lottery teams is invisible to this dataset (it only covers playoff players) — see Kevin Love. Same-team sacrifices (Wade, Manu, Klay) need a different lens.

insights.og_desc: Iguodala gave up 10.8 points of usage and won Finals MVP. Gordon went from Orlando's go-to guy to Denver's fourth option and a ring. 33 stars who won bigger by needing the ball less.

insights.foot: Repeater = tax in 3 of previous 4 seasons (Hoops Rumors repeater tracker). Warriors' $176.9M in 2023-24 is the all-time single-season record; they missed the playoffs that year.
insights.lede: Repeater-rate tax paid in the window, 2015-16 → 2024-25. Golden State's four repeater seasons alone exceed the decade totals of every other franchise — and their 2019-20 duck-under bought them only one non-repeater year.
insights.og_desc: The Warriors' repeater bills alone top every other franchise's decade total — including a record $176.9M for a season they missed the playoffs.
insights.og_title: $531.2M in repeater tax: the price of keeping a dynasty together

insights.title: The Warriors paid $531.2M at repeater rates — including a record $176.9M for a season they missed the playoffs
insights.tldr: Repeater penalties (tax in 3 of 4 seasons) turned the Warriors' dynasty maintenance into the most expensive tax run in NBA history.

insights.foot: Boston $180M = projected tax penalties saved (Bobby Marks, June 2025; Keith Smith estimated ~$196M in total savings). GSW/LAC rows = bill reduction from 2023-24 to 2024-25 after letting Thompson/George walk to duck the apron. KAT = tax saved per the Beacon Journal. Reported by The Ringer, Boston Herald.
insights.lede: Approximate tax savings from apron-driven moves. The second apron doesn't just charge money — it bans the mid-level exception, salary aggregation, and future pick trades, so teams are shedding stars to get under it.
insights.og_desc: Klay walked, PG walked, KAT was dumped, Boston tore apart a title team. The new cap ends dynasties faster than money ever did.
insights.og_title: The second apron broke up contenders in two seasons
insights.stat_label: seasons of the second apron before Boston dismantled a title core
insights.title: The second apron ended dynasties faster than the luxury tax ever did
insights.tldr: Klay Thompson and Paul George walked for nothing, KAT was salary-dumped, and Boston tore apart a title team one summer later — the new cap broke up contenders in two seasons.
insights.viz_label: Approximate tax savings from apron-driven moves ($M)
